title: ARTHUR, Colonel George, Lieutenant-Governor, and MURRAY, Robert Lathrop.
description: ARTHUR, Colonel George, Lieutenant-Governor, and MURRAY, Robert Lathrop. ORIGINAL LAND GRANT TO ROBERT LATHROP MURRAY, of a parcel of land along Upper Goulburn Street to Upper Bathurst Street. Quarto, 350 x 410 mm., printed form on vellum completed in manuscript, signed by Governor Arthur, folded. Hobart Town, 29 August, 1836. Signed by Governor Arthur and John Montagu, Colonial Secretary, with manuscript note on verso regarding the quit rent unpaid at 31st December 1835. + MURRAY, Robert Lathrop. MANUSCRIPT PROMISSORY NOTE, manuscript on a slip of paper, Robert Lathrop Murray to the Derwent Bank, 13 January 1845, for the sum of sixty-seven pounds and ten shillings. Murray (1777-1850) is best known for his editing of The Hobart Town Gazette and The Colonial Times during periods in the 1820s, for his outspoken criticism of Governor Arthur, and for the struggle for freedom of the press. Once the Governor’s attempts to control the VDL press were over-ruled by London, Murray tempered his criticism and eventually became a supporter. In 1828 he commenced publication of Murray’s Austral-Asiatic Review, which continued under changing names and ownership arrangements until the mid 1840s. Estimate $500/700 Illustrated at www.invaluable.com

title: BANKS, Sir Joseph. JOURNAL OF THE RIGHT HON. SIR JOSEPH BANKS... During Captain Cook’s first voyage in H.M.S. Endeavour
description: BANKS, Sir Joseph. JOURNAL OF THE RIGHT HON. SIR JOSEPH BANKS... During Captain Cook’s first voyage in H.M.S. Endeavour in 1768-71… Edited by Sir Joseph D. Hooker. Octavo, with two portraits, and five coloured charts on 4 leaves, uncut in original cloth, gilt, spine faded and rear board striped, with the bookplate of John Davies Enys, and on the rear endpaper the Webster Collection stamp and number. London, Macmillan, 1896. First edition of Banks’s journal. Tipped into this copy is a manuscript letter of 3 pages on a single folded sheet, dated Nov 20/96, from Sir Joseph Hooker to Mr John Davies Enys of Penryn, Cornwall, in which he discusses Henniker Heaton’s ownership and sale of the original Banks journal of the Endeavour voyage, as well as referring to T[homas] Kirk’s Flora of New Zealand. Enys was a New Zealand pastoralist and naturalist. Kirk had moved to New Zealand in 1862 and was appointed chief conservator of forests in 1885. Following his death Hooker wrote “This is a great loss to Botany, for indeed except the late Baron von Mueller there was no other cultivator of Botany in the Southern Hemisphere who could compare with him”. Also, loosely inserted, is a clipped signature of Banks’s fellow botanist Dawson Turner, the father-in-law of Joseph Hooker’s father, William Jackson Hooker. Beddie, 703; Davidson, p. 57; Ferguson, 6635a; Holmes, 92. On Enys see https://teara.govt.nz/en/biographies/2e10/enys-john-davies Estimate $500/800 Illustrated at www.invaluable.com

title: BRISBANE, Sir Thomas, Governor.
description: BRISBANE, Sir Thomas, Governor. ORIGINAL LAND GRANT TO THOMAS GEORGE GREGSON, of 300 acres in the District of Bath, Van Diemen’s Land. Quarto, 320 x 460 mm (excluding seal), manuscript on vellum, signed by Governor Brisbane, with ribbon tie and paper seal, folded, in fine condition. Sydney, 30 June, 1823. Signed by Brisbane, endorsed by Frederick Goulburn, Colonial Secretary. Gregson had migrated from Edinburgh to Van Diemen’s Land in 1823, where he was granted several parcels of land at Jericho and East Risdon. He fostered public and social engagement, becoming a popular local. His interest in hunting and horse-racing led to his organising the first race meeting in the colony. In subsequent decades he was an active voice against transportation, and participated in politics, serving (very briefly) as Premier in 1857. Estimate $400/600 Illustrated at www.invaluable.com

title: COLLINS, David. AN ACCOUNT OF THE ENGLISH COLONY IN NEW SOUTH WALES, from its first Settlement in January 1788, [to Augu
description: COLLINS, David. AN ACCOUNT OF THE ENGLISH COLONY IN NEW SOUTH WALES, from its first Settlement in January 1788, [to August 1801]: with Remarks on the Dispositions, Customs, Manners, &c. of the Native Inhabitants… Two volumes, quarto, with a total of two maps, 23 plates (three handcoloured, uncoloured plates (foxed and offset as usual) and eight half-page engravings (two handcoloured); bound without the half-titles in contemporary calf (rubbed, rebacked and recornered); some foxing or light browning in the text as often. London, Printed by A. Strahan for T. Cadell and W. Davies, 1798-1802. First editions: the extremely scarce complete set of Collins’s great First Fleet narrative. The last of the First Fleet journals to be published but the first history of Australia as an English colony, it is, in its complete form, the most detailed and painstaking of all descriptions of the voyage and first settlement. The fine views of the settlement were engraved in London by Edward Dayes, almost certainly from the sketches of convict artist Thomas Watling. The second volume, notoriously more uncommon than the first, is of great importance, both for its chronicle of later events and for the narratives of voyages and expeditions of discovery undertaken in the intervening years. These include the first printing of Flinders’s log of his northern voyage of 1799 in the Norfolk along the Queensland coast, as far north as Hervey Bay – the first exploration of the coast since Cook and Bligh – as well as the inland expeditions of John Price and Henry Hacking that include “the first report of the existence of the koala, the earliest recorded sighting of a wombat on mainland Australia and the first report of the discovery of the lyre-bird, which is for the first time described and illustrated in colour” (Wantrup). With an interesting marginal note by the original owner in the second volume, citing a report in the London Star newspaper, of 29 August, 1803: “The American Ship Fanny early in the present year sailed through Bass Streights, which separate Van Dieman’s Land from New South Wales, in her passage from Port Jackson to Batavia. The discovery of this passage is of considerable advantage to the commerce of that part of the world”. Ferguson 263 and 350; Wantrup 19-20; Wilson 22-23. Estimate $3000/5000 Illustrated at www.invaluable.com

title: DUTTON, Henry Hampden.
description: DUTTON, Henry Hampden. ACROSS AUSTRALIA BY MOTOR. Rare: only edition of this private publication produced for family use as a record of the first crossing of the continent by automobile. Dutton, a scion of the notable Adelaide family, made this historic trip from Adelaide to Port Darwin accompanied by his mechanic, Murray Aunger, in a 25-horsepower Clement-Talbot over 51 days between 30 June and 20 August, 1908. In a 1975 letter from the author’s daughter, Helen Dutton, she noted the intriguing fact that “Many of his best photos disappeared mysteriously before the book could be printed”. description: FORSTER, Johann Reinhold, Georg Adam Forster, and Anders Sparrman. title: MACQUARIE. GREAT BRITAIN & IRELAND, Parliament.
description: MACQUARIE. GREAT BRITAIN & IRELAND, Parliament. REPORT FROM THE SELECT COMMITTEE ON TRANSPORTATION. Foolscap folio, pp. 118, fine copy in recent navy half calf over buckram boards, in a matching bookform box. [London], Ordered, by The House of Commons, to be Printed, 10 July 1812. A notably rare and important paper, the first of only three contemporary published documents illustrating New South Wales under Lachlan Macquarie, the greatest of the early governors. In 1811, following the deposition of Governor Bligh, there was enough uncertainty in Britain about the value of the transportation of convicts to New South Wales for a Parliamentary Select Committee to be formed to inquire into the system which had operated since 1787 and to recommend future policy. The Report includes a complete transcript of the evidence given by many notable witnesses, including former Governor John Hunter (twelve pages), former Governor William Bligh (19 pages), his deposer George Johnston (three pages), Scottish Martyr Maurice Margarot, Matthew Flinders, First Fleet chaplain Richard Johnson, and many other colonial officials. Extracts from several of Macquarie’s early dispatches are included. It endorsed the existing system of transportation and “the liberal views of the present Governor”, and became effectively the foundation for Macquarie’s programme of civil and administrative improvement. Ferguson, 543; Wantrup, 38. Estimate $1200/2200 Illustrated at www.invaluable.com

This important document contains a long despatch from Macquarie to Lord Bathurst, dated 28th June 1813, in which he explains his early progress in reforming the colony. Ferguson, 646. title: MACQUARIE. GREAT BRITAIN & IRELAND, Parliament.
description: MACQUARIE. GREAT BRITAIN & IRELAND, Parliament. REPORT FROM THE SELECT COMMITTEE ON THE STATE OF GAOLS, &C. [London], House of Commons, Ordered to be printed 12 July, 1819. Rare: the third of three contemporary published documents illustrating New South Wales under Lachlan Macquarie. This important report was a key prelude to Bigge’s destruction of Macquarie, provides one of the most detailed accounts of the colony prior to Bigge’s arrival (see Wantrup pp. 142-143, where the background and consequences of this important report are discussed). Among those to give evidence were Alexander Riley, Jeffery Hart Bent, Samuel Bate, and John Macarthur. Ferguson, 747; Wantrup, 43. Estimate $600/900 Illustrated at www.invaluable.com

title: MACQUARIE. BIGGE, John Thomas.
description: MACQUARIE. BIGGE, John Thomas. REPORT OF THE COMMISSIONER OF INQUIRY INTO THE STATE OF THE COLONY OF NEW SOUTH WALES. Foolscap folio, pp. [iv], 186 + [2]; fine, crisp copy in more recent cloth. [London], House of Commons, Ordered to be printed 19 June 1822. Rare suppressed first issue of Bigge’s first report with the libellous remarks about W.C. Wentworth that were omitted from the subsequent corrected House of Commons printing and the House of Lords printing. “As initially printed in June 1822, the first report contained a libellous and unproven reference to William Wentworth on pages 148-149. The first printing of the report was withdrawn and a new printing, excluding these remarks, was ordered by the House of Commons, to be printed on 5 August 1822” (Cains). This is a pleasing and distinctly appropriate copy, with the added contemporary printed leaf, “This book is to be preserved in the Office of the Lords Commissioners of His Majesty’s Treasury 1822 [-1823]”, and with the neat stamp of the Public Record Office in the bottom margin of the facing leaf dated in the first and second years of the reign of Queen Victoria; released in 2008. Cains, 11; Ferguson, 854; Wantrup, 46. John Thomas Bigge (1780-1843) was appointed Royal Commissioner, with sweeping powers, by Lord Bathurst to examine the transportation system, but “it was clear that Macquarie’s administration as much as the transportation system was under review. From the moment of his arrival in the colony in 1819 Bigge’s relations with Macquarie were strained. As time wore on the tension turned to antipathy and Bigge found himself more in sympathy with the exclusives of the squattocracy than with the Governor. Bigge was assiduous in assembling evidence in New South Wales and Van Diemen’s Land, but he was far from judicious and impartial in his methods of collecting it and in the prejudicial conclusions he drew. His series of reports were published in 1822 and 1823. By that time Macquarie had resigned... Bigge’s reports had a profound influence on the future constitutional and political development of Australia and have a place in any Australian collection...” (Wantrup). Beside dealing with the question of Macquarie’s competence, the reports contain most important and detailed evidence about life and conditions in the early 1820s, at that crucial point when the colony began to leave behind its penal past and look to the pioneer emigrant for its future. It was also as a direct result of Bigge’s reports that the Moreton Bay area was first explored with a view to future settlement. Bigge had urged the Colonial Office to seek places away from Sydney both to send intractable offenders and to encourage free settlement by releasing land for graziers. Consequently, Oxley was commissioned by Brisbane to reconnoitre the north coast. He explored Moreton Bay and named the Brisbane River; his report ultimately led to the foundation of the Moreton Bay colony. Estimate $500/800 Illustrated at www.invaluable.com

title: PHILLIP, Captain Arthur, Governor.
description: PHILLIP, Captain Arthur, Governor. THE VOYAGE OF GOVERNOR PHILLIP TO BOTANY BAY; with an Account of the Establishment of the Colonies of Port Jackson and Norfolk Island... to which are added the Journals of Lieuts. Shortland, Watts, Ball and Capt. Marshall. Quarto, with 54 engraved plates and charts, bound in contemporary calf, sympathetically rebacked, retaining the original endpapers, all edges yellow. London, John Stockdale, 1789. First edition of the foundation book for New South Wales. The officially sanctioned account of the new colony, it is a full record of events both on land and on sea in the first months of the settlement from March 1787, just before the First Fleet sailed, up to September 1788. The text records the early expeditions of Phillip and the other officers into the interior around Botany Bay and Port Jackson, and the earliest coastal voyages of discovery. Text and plates illustrate newly discovered animal life, and among the charts and plans (most notably by John Hunter and William Dawes) is the earliest plan of the settlement at Sydney Cove, showing what buildings and other progress had been made there by July 1788. Finally, although far from complete, an appendix lists the convicts embarked on the First Fleet. In this copy the plate at page 150 is in the rare “Wulpine” state; the engraved title is in the second state. Ayer/Zimmer, 491; Davidson, pp. 70-2; Ferguson, 47; Hill 2, 1347; Wantrup, 5a. Estimate $2000/2800 Illustrated at www.invaluable.com

title: SCOTT, Robert Falcon. SCOTT’S LAST EXPEDITION In Two Volumes.
description: SCOTT, Robert Falcon. SCOTT’S LAST EXPEDITION In Two Volumes. Volume I. Being the Journals of Captain R.F. Scott...Volume II. Being the Reports of the Journeys & the Scientific Work undertaken by Dr. E. A. Scott had attained the South Pole on 18 January, 1912, having been beaten by Amundsen just over a month earlier. But it is the disastrous return journey that made this failed expedition so poignant, with Scott, Oates, Evans, Bowers, and Wilson all dying before reaching safety. title: STIRLING, Sir James. JOURNALS OF SEVERAL EXPEDITIONS MADE IN WESTERN AUSTRALIA, during the years 1829, 1830, 1831, and 1
description: STIRLING, Sir James. JOURNALS OF SEVERAL EXPEDITIONS MADE IN WESTERN AUSTRALIA, during the years 1829, 1830, 1831, and 1832. Duodecimo, large folding engraved map (a couple of expert paper repairs at folds) as frontispiece, with the advertisement leaf, an attractive copy, uncut in original cloth, modern rebacking and paper spine label. A FINE ASSOCIATION COPY of this rare and important title: with the signature of Charles Stirling, presumably Major Charles Edward Stirling, one of Sir James’s four sons, born January 1834. First edition: undertaken on Sir James Stirling’s orders, the inland explorations recorded here effectively made known the principal outlines for future settlement in Western Australia. The major success of Stirling’s governorship came from the coastal surveys and inland expeditions he sent out or undertook himself for the encouragement of new settlements. “The earliest work relating to the inland exploration of Western Australia. The book consists of the journals and reports of over twenty exploratory expeditions into the country around the Swan River settlement undertaken by, among others, the colony’s Surveyor General, John Septimus Roe, and the artist and Assistant Surveyor, Robert Dale. Cross edited their journals for publication and draughted a fine map from them which is included in the volume” (Wantrup). On the frontispiece map is the publisher’s announcement that a large and more detailed version had been published by Cross’s greater contemporary, Arrowsmith. Ferguson, 1664; Wantrup, 151; Tooley, 360. Estimate $6000/9000 Illustrated at www.invaluable.com

title: WEBB PRINTING CO. COMPLETE SET OF SUGGESTIVE POSTCARDS, forming a striptease sequence.
description: WEBB PRINTING CO. COMPLETE SET OF SUGGESTIVE POSTCARDS, forming a striptease sequence. Ten colour lithograph postcards, fine. (Melbourne, Webb Printing, circa 1910). A complete set of this series of suggestive or erotic, numbered, colour-printed postcards: rare, only one set traced in Australian institutions (SLV). “We, the royal we, have written before about the absence of colonial Australian pornography and the rarity of even a hint of the erotic. In book or picture these postcards are as racy it gets. Still, they are about sex and desire, not the overflowing bottoms and bosoms, the slap and tickle, that make for a saucy English postcard” (Richard Neylon). “The uncaptioned sequence shows a young lady of Edwardian times apparently preparing for an assignation with a lover. The sequence, which as Richard Neylon astutely observed is based on (probably French) photographs, is by no means pornographic but it is erotic, in the widest, most generous, and perhaps tamest sense of the word – saucy rather than salacious. Nonetheless, as one of very few extant examples of Australian-produced ‘erotica’ of the Edwardian or Victorian eras, this Webb series is an object of considerable bibliophilic, cartophilic, and sociological interest” (Jonathan Wantrup in Australian Rare Books 1901-1950, forthcoming). Estimate $300/500 Illustrated at www.invaluable.com
